title: manuf: simplify API, constify types
description:
* manuf: constify API, improve internal documentation

    * None of the OUI tables are supposed to be written to, constify them.
    * Use proper types in the bsearch parameters to avoid confusion.
    * Move masking outside the bsearch function as tiny optimization.
    * Document the MA-L/M/S macros.

* manuf: simplify ws_manuf_iter_next API

    * Remove an internal implementation from the public API. Now the result
      is propagated as second parameter while the return value indicates
      whether an entry was found.
    * Change iteration function to avoid comparing string pointers, two
      different values may or may not point to the same underlying value
      depending on linker optimization.

* manuf: change ws_manuf_lookup return type to bool

    The result was propagated through both the return value and the first
    output parameter. Change the return type to indicate whether it matched.

notes.body: requested review from @jvalverde

I pondered with the following optimization, but did not implement them:

```diff
- { { 0x00, 0x55, 0xDA, 0x00 }, "ShinkoTechno", "Shinko Technos co.,ltd." }
+ E(0055DA00, "ShinkoTechno", "Shinko Technos co.,ltd.")
```
With a macro being
```
#defined E(oui28, short_name, long_name) { 0x ## oui28, short_name, long_name },
```
and maybe some shenanigans for byte order.

And instead of `uint8_t oui24[3]`, we would have `uint32_t` or even `uint64_t`. Due to alignment reasons, `uint8_t[3]`, `uint8_t[4]`, and `uint8_t[5]` would all be the same as `uint64_t` on 64-bit systems. With that change, and with appropriate masking, we can replace the the `memcmp` by a simple direct integer comparison using `==`. And if all three OUI structures are basically the same type, we can just use a single data type for them. I am ignoring 32-bit systems for the moment, they cannot use a single data type if we want to use the minimum size possible.

Another thing I noticed is that we have a lot of relocations that are handled by the linker due to the many strings. The advantage of this is that duplicate values (such as `"Xerox"`) can be combined into a single value. In theory we could do this by ourselves, build one gigantic character array with `\0`-terminated strings. E.g. `"Xerox\0Xerox Corporation\0etc"`. And then instead of storing `const char *`, we would store one or two offsets into this big table. That could potentially result in significant binary savings because we would save on:

 - Less linker relocation entries.
 - Instead of two 64-bit pointers. we would have a single 32-bit offset for every manuf entry.
 - There would be one extra indirection needed for looking up the names, a minor trade-off I think?

For this optimization, it would be best if we store a text file in the Git repo again, and generate the C code during the build.

Thoughts on these? @jvalverde
My thought is that the benefit seems negligible and I don't see big space savings anywhere. The compiler, at least GCC, already stores repeated static strings as a single value.

Why remove `ws_manuf_iter_init()` and then put it in a comment?

The change to `ws_manuf_iter_next()` not taking an array of size 3 is positive, but changing the return argument isn't. A lookup function is supposed to return the item being looked up. The fact that it also takes a pointer to static memory as an argument is incidental to the implementation.

The comment is there just to ensure that people are not doing stupid stuff. Unfortunately, C has uninitialized memory. In Go, this pattern of starting from a "default" value is quite common, and I liked removing this function because it does not add much over the convention of zero-initializing a value.

Sure, I can restore the return value, I will make it `const struct ws_manuf *` then. I will then also remove the second argument and move it to the `struct ws_manuf_iter` type since it is an internal implementation detail that would allow the memory to remain valid after returning. Is that ok to you?

I don't know that the memory remains valid, because it is now tied to the lifetime of the iterator. How is that a win? Note that I did not say "internal" detail. I said "incidental" to the implementation, i.e. the caller is free to choose how that memory is allocated (typically on the stack but not necessarily). The alternative would be to return malloc'ed memory and that buffer argument then disappears.

And I see no reason to remove the iter initialization function. Can you keep it please? It's a common pattern and it ensures memory is initialized and it can be useful in the future to change the implementation without breaking the API.

I would really prefer the zero initialization pattern without new APIs that do exactly the same, but that's not a hill I want to die on. I'll restore it in the next change.

On the return value of the iterator, I considered reverting the "bool" return type to a pointer, but decided not to do so. Previously the pointer was needed as an artifact of the previous implementation. We can however have interface now where we signal whether the end of the list is reached or not (through a `bool` return value), and provide values through parameters.

Here is another data structure and API that follows this pattern, one that also has an init function: https://docs.gtk.org/glib/method.HashTableIter.next.html
```
gboolean
g_hash_table_iter_next (
  GHashTableIter* iter,
  gpointer* key,
  gpointer* value
)
```

It's a silly preference. The iter init function makes the requirement to initialize the iterator explicit ("initialize", not "zero-initialize"). And empty initializers are a GNU extension in C11.

I was thinking of the return value of `ws_manuf_lookup()`. I don't have a strong opinion on ws_manuf_iter_next(). Returning `bool` is fine.

```
WS_DLL_PUBLIC
struct ws_manuf *
ws_manuf_lookup(const uint8_t addr[6], struct ws_manuf *buf);

WS_DLL_PUBLIC
void
ws_manuf_iter_init(ws_manuf_iter_t *iter);

WS_DLL_PUBLIC
bool
ws_manuf_iter_next(ws_manuf_iter_t *iter, struct ws_manuf *result);
```

Even if a completely empty initializer is a GNU extension, you can still zero-initialize an aggregate type (array/struct) by initializing the first member to zero. See 13, 17, 21 of 6.7.9. Initialization of C99, https://open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf.

If you really feel strongly about not returning a boolean from the lookup function, I can drop that last commit.

Edit: oh, it looks like you already merged it! Sorry for the late reply here, I had a meeting :sweat_smile: .
I changed it in !11884. Have a look.
I think this is a `uint8_t *`.
You are right. I will change the naming to make this clearer. I was confused by a similar pattern that can be found in hash tables.

Maybe you could split the commits, it would help. If not I can manage.

I can split it, what would you propose? Constify the tables, change the iterator implementation, and the lookup implementation?

Less/more splits?
Yes, I was thinking exactly that. Constify, change the iterator implementation to remove the manuf[NUM_REGISTRIES] argument (thumbs up to that), then everything else.
